section: 5. Regression Eval You Can Actually Gate On — A/B
quote: **Block** automatically, and only, on deterministic contract properties: schema conformance, required disclaimers, banned claims, brand-name spelling, length bounds, no personal data echoed, latency, cost.
problem: The schema in §2B declares a `criticality_class` field ('is this output criterion-referenceable (structured, checkable) or holistic (copy, tone)?') and §5A ends with 'That is what `criticality_class` records' — but the field is then given no operational consequence anywhere. The blanket 'and only' rule makes it decorative: if the policy is identical for both classes, nothing turns on recording the class, and a builder cannot implement it. The eval interim states the opposite as its own boundary condition: the block/report split 'does NOT hold with the same force for criterion-referenceable prompt outputs inside the same registry (e.g., a prompt producing structured data extraction, a classification label, or a templated document with checkable fields) — there ... a well-specified LLM judge can plausibly support a soft-block gate, and the product should let the human define per-prompt-family which regime applies rather than applying one policy universally' (interim-eval-gate, Boundary conditions). The supporting numbers are in the same interim: structured questions fMAE ≈0.22 with ρ>0.6 blind, committee ρ=0.885 with the official solution supplied, plots ρ>0.84. The report cites those numbers in §5A and then discards the design conclusion they license.
fix: Make `criticality_class` load-bearing. Rewrite the Block rule as a two-regime rule rather than a universal one: deterministic contract properties block for every asset; for assets whose `criticality_class` is criterion-referenceable (structured extraction, classification, templated documents with checkable fields) a judge score may additionally soft-block, since on that regime discrimination is real — ρ>0.6 blind, committee ρ=0.885 with a reference answer supplied [criterion-referenceability-determines-llm-as-a-judge-validity-across-physics-ass]; for holistic assets (copy, tone, brand voice) the judge never scores and never blocks, only selects divergence examples. State that the approver sets the regime per prompt family at first promotion, which is the field's whole purpose. This also removes an internal contradiction between §2B and §5B at roughly the words it costs.

section: 5. Regression Eval You Can Actually Gate On — A
quote: discrimination is already poor at ρ≈0.1, and a mark scheme does not improve it (ρ≈0, all confidence intervals including zero)
problem: The report omits the intervention a builder will actually reach for and the trap that comes with it. The eval interim records that anchored few-shot exemplars were tested too and also failed (committee blind ρ=0.088, scheme ρ=−0.044, scheme+anchor ρ=0.034, 'every single one of these 95% CIs includes zero'), and — the load-bearing part — that anchoring produces a false signal of success: it 'compress[es] the AI score distribution below even the human standard deviation' and pulls the mean within 2.3 marks of the human mean, so 'distributional agreement can occur without valid discrimination' (interim-eval-gate). A team that adds anchor examples, sees MAE fall and the score histogram line up with human scores, will conclude the judge is now validated. The report's current phrasing leaves that specific self-deception uncovered, and it is exactly the mistake this product's evidence card would encode.
fix: Replace the mark-scheme clause with one that carries both interventions and the trap: neither a written mark scheme nor anchored exemplars improves discrimination (committee ρ=−0.044 and 0.034, every 95% CI spanning zero); anchoring only compresses the AI score distribution toward the human mean, so low absolute error and a well-aligned score histogram are not evidence of validity [criterion-referenceability-determines-llm-as-a-judge-validity-across-physics-ass]. Costs roughly a dozen words and closes the one route by which a builder would reintroduce the scalar score the design refuses.

section: 6. The Promote Gate — B. The legal basis, stated correctly
quote: Separately, for any system operating before 1 March 2026, transitioning organizations must submit a notice on the one-stop portal with a transition plan or compliance scheme "within 60 days from the effective date of the Decree (i.e., before June 30, 2026)"
problem: Stated unconditionally, and then relied on as accomplished fact in the closing section ('with a 60-day notification clock already run'). The promote-gate interim reads the Decree's operative mechanics differently and more precisely: risk classification into three tiers 'must occur "before putting the system into operation" (Decree Art. 5, per Law Art. 9), via self-assessment or a conformity-assessment body; only medium- and high-risk systems must be notified to the Ministry of Science and Technology via a one-stop portal — low-risk systems face no notification requirement' (interim-promote-gate). The notification duty is therefore conditional on a classification the group must perform itself, and for a low-risk system there is no clock at all. This is the one place in the report where a reader may take a dated compliance action, and the precondition that decides whether the action is owed is missing.
fix: Qualify the 60-day clock with its trigger: it attaches to systems the deployer has classified medium- or high-risk (classification is a self-assessment or conformity-assessment done before the system goes into operation; low-risk systems carry no notification duty) [update-decree-1422026nd-cp-guiding-the-artificial-intelligence-law-in-vietnam-vi]. Then soften the closing section's 'already run' to reflect that the clock runs only for classified medium/high-risk systems, so the real first action is classification, not notification. Roughly 25 words, and it turns an assertion a counsel would strike into an implementable step.

section: 6. The Promote Gate — B. The legal basis, stated correctly / 12. Audited absences
quote: Neither regime obliges a pre-release human sign-off on an internal prompt-management layer, and getting this wrong would not survive counsel review.
problem: A two-jurisdiction negative claim, used in the lead paragraph to reframe one of the four hard constraints, rests on an evidence base that explicitly did not read the EU article most on point. The promote-gate interim states it plainly: 'The EU Act's actual human-oversight article is Art. 14 (not in my read set this round)', and the digest carries the same flag: 'Article 14 of the EU AI Act (human oversight, as opposed to Article 12 logging) not read directly in this pass' (interim-promote-gate; evidence-digest 6.5). The report's audited-absences list carries five items and this is not one of them, so the claim reads as fully verified when its own interim rates it medium confidence. Under the run's provenance discipline, an audited absence asserted without stating what was searched is a finding.
fix: Add one clause where the EU side is stated — that the EU claim rests on Article 12 (record-keeping) read directly, while Article 14 (human oversight) was not read in this pass, so the EU half is held at medium confidence — and add the same line to the audited-absences list in §12. Alternatively narrow the lead sentence from 'no statutory basis ... in either jurisdiction examined' to 'no statutory basis found in the provisions examined'. Under ten words if done in the lead, ~20 if done properly in both places.

section: 1. What the Asset Framing Commits You To — C
quote: Two caveats sharpen it: the corpus is 72.8% public prompt-collection repositories whose purpose is aggregating popular prompts, so the *external* figures plausibly reflect benign convergence rather than organizational waste
problem: The caveat is applied at repository level, but the report's most eye-catching number — 38.5% prompt-level semantic duplication across 24,800 prompts — is a prompt-level figure, and the registry-decay interim records the fact that guts it: 'the top eight repositories accounting for 90.8% of the collected data', with 'the six largest repositories are all categorized as prompt collections' (interim-registry-decay-design-lessons, §7). The 38.5% is therefore very close to a measurement of eight prompt-collection dumps, not of 92 organizations' working practice. The report currently protects the external repo-level figures with this caveat and leaves the prompt-level headline unprotected, which is where a sceptical reader will attack the founding premise.
fix: Extend the existing caveat to name the prompt-level concentration rather than only the repo-level composition: the eight largest repositories supply 90.8% of the 24,800 prompts and the six largest are all prompt collections, so the 38.5% prompt-level figure largely measures collection dumps [understanding-prompt-management-in-github-repositories-a-call-for-best-practices]. This can replace the existing '72.8% ... benign convergence' clause almost word-for-word rather than sitting alongside it, since it makes the same point more sharply and at the level where the number was cited.

section: 9. The Agent Layer — C. The agent, narrowed rather than dropped
quote: The harm is dimension-specific — the same edit improved instruction-following — so there is no scalar better prompt.
problem: The report cites the 26/30→9/30 collapse but drops the four-condition ablation that says *what to forbid*, which is the only part a builder can act on. The agent-scope interim records it precisely: 'adding the system wrapper alone (A→B) has no effect — all metrics remain identical. Adding generic rules to the user prompt (B→C) causes extraction degradation in Llama 3 (100%→90%)... RAG performance degrades across both models when the full improved prompt is used' (interim-agent-scope, quoting the full-text v1). The damage is localized to generic rules appended to the user prompt; a system-level wrapper was inert. That converts a general warning into a concrete constraint on the exception-reporter's output space, which is precisely the decision §9C is asking the reader to make.
fix: Add the ablation's localization to the existing sentence: the four-condition ablation isolates it — a generic system wrapper alone changed nothing, while appending generic rules to the user prompt is what degraded grounding [when-better-prompts-hurt-evaluation-driven-iteration-for-llm-applications-a-fram]. Then draw the build rule the report already implies but never states: the exception reporter may propose task-specific contract language, never generic helpfulness rules appended to the user prompt. ~25 words for a directly implementable constraint.

section: 4. Versioning, Release, and Rollback Mechanics — C
quote: Client software development kits (SDKs) cache prompts with a default time-to-live of 60 seconds and revalidate in the background, so running instances serve the rolled-back version within roughly one cache interval
problem: The 60-second figure is correct but presented as a fixed property of the world, when the source documents it as a per-fetch parameter: 'The default cache TTL (Time To Live) is 60 seconds', configurable per call (the docs show `cache_ttl_seconds=300`, and `0` to disable caching entirely) [caching-langfuse]. Since the report's own design rule is that 'the gate is only defensible to a non-engineer if undo is one click and takes effect in seconds', the fact that rollback latency is a knob the register can set per consumer — and can tighten for high-blast-radius prompts at the price of extra network calls — is the actionable half of the paragraph, and it is missing.
fix: Recast the sentence so the number is a lever rather than a constant: the SDK cache TTL defaults to 60 seconds and is set per fetch (0 disables caching, higher values reduce network overhead) [caching-langfuse], so rollback wall-clock is a register-side policy — a shorter TTL for prompts whose `consumers[]` blast radius is large, the default elsewhere — and the figure the card shows is per-consumer, not universal. Roughly length-neutral against the current sentence plus its follow-on.

section: 3. Ingestion — B. Do not build clustering on hashing alone
quote: Design rule: MinHash as a cheap pre-filter, embedding similarity at a high cosine threshold for the semantic pass, which is what the GitHub study used
problem: This is the section's actual build instruction and it is the vaguest sentence in it. 'A high cosine threshold' is not implementable; the parameters exist in the evidence and cost the same number of words. The registry-decay interim verified them against the paper: 'we assess semantic duplication via sentence embeddings (using "all-mpnet-base-v2") with a cosine similarity threshold of >0.95' (interim-registry-decay-design-lessons, §7). Clustering is the report's standing compensating control for an architecture that cannot merge, so its threshold is a decision the reader must make.
fix: Substitute the parameters for the adjective: MinHash as a cheap pre-filter, then a sentence-embedding pass at cosine >0.95 — the exact configuration (all-mpnet-base-v2, >0.95) the GitHub study used [understanding-prompt-management-in-github-repositories-a-call-for-best-practices]. Optionally note this is the tunable that decides whether near-duplicates surface as one asset or as deliberate variants, tying it to `cluster_id`. Word-for-word swap at the same length.

section: 3. Ingestion — A. Three methods / 12. Audited absences
quote: The gap between the two is exactly the document-and-chat estate, so **document-source connectors are a structurally required third method, not an optional integration**
problem: The two methods the report *doesn't* rely on come with documented methodology (AST parsing across seven languages, CycloneDX v1.4 Prompt SBOM with hash and file/line; egress observation of known model endpoints). The one it declares structurally required — and which is the lead differentiator, the first build phase, and the first demo beat — is given no mechanism at all: nothing about what a Notion/Sheets/Drive connector reads, how a prompt candidate is distinguished from ordinary prose in a document, or how a chat export is segmented. The corpus does not supply one either (interim-registry-decay and interim-adoption both note no source covers internal document-estate prompt discovery; the run's audited absence #2/#3 cover related gaps). The report should carry that as an audited absence rather than let the strongest-sounding sentence in the section be the least supported.
fix: Add a half-sentence naming the asymmetry: the two methods with published methodologies are the two that cannot see the target estate, while the required third has no methodological precedent in the record — candidate extraction from documents and chat exports is unspecified anywhere and is the design's largest unevidenced dependency. Add the same line to the §12 audited-absences list, where the near-identical point is already made about the differentiator's efficacy ('No source shows any competitor doing it') but not about its method.

section: 10. Adoption Inside the Organization — A / 11. Build Sequence
quote: "the most common migration failure is asking a team to abandon a working tool before the replacement can do what the tool does,"
problem: The adoption interim carries a four-step migration roadmap and the report keeps only step one. The three dropped steps are the only rollout mechanics in the whole evidence base and the build sequence in §11 has no rollout plan at all: '(2) migrate live data, not just structure — "Teams will abandon a new system the moment they need information that only exists in the old one"; (3) assign a transition owner per migrated process — the person who ran the shadow spreadsheet validates coverage and "flag[s] any gap that appears during the first four weeks"; (4) enforce single source of truth from the first live use — "if it is not in the system, it does not exist for decision-making purposes"' (interim-adoption, §3). Step 2 is a direct instruction to the ingestion design (sweep the live Sheet, not a schema); step 3 names a role the pilot needs and nobody has assigned; step 4 is the mandate condition §10C says a conglomerate plausibly has. For a query asking how to solve the problem, this is the deployment half of the answer.
fix: Compress the three missing steps into one sentence in §10A or as a pilot line in §11: migrate the live content rather than the structure, name a transition owner per migrated team who validates coverage and flags gaps through the first four weeks, and declare single-source-of-truth from first live use — if it is not in the register it does not count for decisions [how-hidden-spreadsheets-shadow-workflows-drain-budgets-mtm-blog]. ~40 words; it can be paid for by trimming the §10B table's 'What compensates' prose, which restates points made in §10A.

section: 6. The Promote Gate — A. The delivery-performance attack
quote: Two defences follow: at most one active candidate version per prompt awaiting decision, and instrumentation of time-to-decision and override rate.
problem: The report elsewhere makes rubber-stamp instrumentation one of its three falsification instruments, so the detector's definition matters. The source's actual leading indicator is a joint condition, not two independent metrics: 'Very short latency combined with fast approvals may indicate reviews are not happening at all', alongside a named metric, 'Thorough Review Rate' (interim-agent-scope, quoting rubber-stamp-reviews-minware). Time-to-decision alone is ambiguous — a fast decision on a pre-computed card is the design's intended outcome, which is exactly why the conjunction with approval rate is what discriminates a working gate from a theatrical one.
fix: State the detector as the conjunction the source gives: short time-to-decision together with a near-100% approval rate is the rubber-stamp signature, whereas short time-to-decision with a live rejection rate is the card working as designed [rubber-stamp-reviews-minware]. Pairs naturally with §12's edit-rate-on-purpose-field instrument. Roughly length-neutral against the current clause.
